This vignette shows the steps of a simulation study: fit a model to data, simulate a new data set
from the fitted model, refit the model to the simulated data, and compare the estimates with the
true parameters.

## The true model

We fit a logistic growth curve to the heights of the faba beans in `FabaHeights25`, with random
effects on the asymptote b1, the time of the maximum growth rate b2 and the scale b3 of each plant.
The random effects of a plant are correlated: their covariance matrix is unstructured. The threshold
b4 and the asymmetry b5 are fixed at their defaults, b4 = 0 (the curve starts at zero at time 0) and
b5 = 1 (the symmetric curve).

```{r fit}
library(gcTMB)
library(ggplot2)

fit <- gcTMB(height ~ DAS, rform = b1 + b2 + b3 ~ 1 | plant_ID, data = FabaHeights25)
fit
converged(fit)

```

The fitted model is the true model of the simulation. Its parameters are:

```{r truth}
fixef(fit)
VarCorr(fit)
sigma(fit)
```

Other true models can be made from it with `update()`, e.g. `update(fit, fixef = c(b1 = 150))`
for a larger asymptote, or `update(fit, VarCorr = ...)` for other covariance matrices of the
random effects.

## Simulation

We simulate 50 new plants, each measured at 10 equidistant days from day 5 to day 100. Each plant
in `newdata` is a new curve, with its own random effects drawn from the fitted covariance matrix.

```{r simulate}
simdata <- expand.grid(DAS = seq(5, 100, length.out = 10),
                       plant_ID = paste("plant", 1:50, sep = ""))
simdata$height <- simulate(fit, nsim = 1, seed = 1, newdata = simdata)[[1]]
head(simdata)
```

## Refitting the model

The same model is fitted to the simulated data.

```{r refit}
simfit <- gcTMB(height ~ DAS, rform = b1 + b2 + b3 ~ 1 | plant_ID, data = simdata)
converged(simfit)
```

The 95% profile confidence intervals of the coefficients and the variance parameters are compared
with the true values, the estimates of the original fit. `confint` reports the standard deviations
of the random effects and the residual standard deviation on their natural scale, while `coef` has
them on the log scale, so the true values and the estimates are transformed in the same way. The
correlations of the three random effects stay on the unconstrained scale of `coef`.

```{r confint}
ci <- confint(simfit,method="boot",nsim=50)
natural <- function(p){
  lg <- grepl("^log_", names(p))
  p[lg] <- exp(p[lg])
  p
}
truth <- natural(coef(fit))
tab <- data.frame(true = truth, estimate = natural(coef(simfit)), ci,
                  covered = truth >= ci[, 1] & truth <= ci[, 2],
                  check.names = FALSE)
# the standard deviations are on their natural scale: drop "log_" from their names
rownames(tab) <- sub("^log_", "", rownames(tab))
tab
```

In a full simulation study, these steps are repeated for many simulated data sets, e.g. to estimate
the coverage of the confidence intervals or to compare growth models with `criteria()`.

## Plot

The simulated heights and the estimated curves of the 50 plants:

```{r plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5}
grid <- expand.grid(DAS = seq(5, 100, length.out = 200), plant_ID = unique(simdata$plant_ID))
grid$height <- predict(simfit, newdata = grid)

ggplot(simdata, aes(DAS, height, group = plant_ID)) +
  geom_line(data = grid, colour = "grey50", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Days after sowing", y = "Height") +
  theme_bw()
```
